summary: Gives an overview of terminology and definitions used for two Information-Centric Networking architectures, Named Data Networking (NDN) and Content-Centric Networking (CCNx). In these, communication works by requesting named content rather than sending to addresses.

plainLanguage.summary: CCNx and Named Data Networking request content by name rather than sending packets to a destination address. This RFC explains terms used for the shared ideas and different components in those two architectures.

questions: what is ndn and ccnx terminology
how are data packets signed in icn
how do interest and data packets work
subtitle: A shared vocabulary for the CCNx and Named Data Networking architectures.

tldr.problem: Information-Centric Networking uses names to request data, but CCNx and Named Data Networking have developed overlapping terms for related concepts.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC collects terms used in the CCNx and NDN projects and groups them by nodes, forwarding, packets, names, and data-centric security.
tldr.outcome: It provides an informational terminology reference for these two ICN architectures; other ICN designs are outside its scope.

today: RFC 8793 is an Informational IRTF document published in June 2020. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Information-Centric Networking
sections.content:
Information-Centric Networking (ICN) makes named data the focus of communication. Instead of sending a packet to a destination address, a consumer requests data using its name. The network can deliver data from a source or a copy stored along the path.

Named Data Networking (NDN) and Content-Centric Networking (CCNx) are two ICN architectures. This RFC collects the terminology used to describe concepts in those projects; it does not cover other ICN architectures.
sections.plainLanguage: In ICN, a consumer requests data by name instead of sending to a device address. This document collects terminology used by the NDN and CCNx projects.

sections.title: Interest and Data Packets
sections.content:
An Interest packet requests data using a name or name prefix. A Data packet carries content that matches the request. When more than one Data packet could match, the network returns one matching packet for that Interest.

Data packets bind names to content using cryptographic means, such as a signature or an implicit name derived from a cryptographic hash. A valid binding shows that the content matches the name, but the consumer still needs a trust model to decide whether the source is trustworthy.
sections.plainLanguage: An Interest asks for named data, and a matching Data packet carries the answer. A cryptographic binding can show that the name matches the content, but does not by itself establish trust in the source.

sections.title: Nodes and Forwarding State
sections.content:
An ICN node can act as a consumer, a producer, or a forwarder. A forwarder uses a Forwarding Information Base (FIB) to choose where to send Interests, a Pending Interest Table (PIT) to record unsatisfied requests, and a Content Store (CS) to cache data.

When an Interest arrives, a forwarder checks whether its cache can satisfy it. If not, it records the Interest and forwards it based on its FIB and forwarding strategy. When matching Data returns, the PIT helps forward it to the requesting interface.
sections.plainLanguage: A forwarder can store data, remember requests that are waiting for answers, and choose where to send new requests. Its cache may answer a request without contacting a producer.

sections.title: Names, Prefixes, and Segments
sections.content:
An ICN name is a sequence of components and is often hierarchical and meaningful to an application. A prefix name contains only the start of a longer name and can be used to find matching forwarding information. A full name can include a packet identifier derived from the Data packet.

Large application data can be split into multiple Data packets with a shared name prefix and different segment components. A version component can distinguish revisions of an object. The name structure is therefore used both to identify data and to organize requests.
sections.plainLanguage: A name identifies data and may have several components arranged in a hierarchy. Large objects can be split into named segments, and a version component can distinguish revisions.

sections.title: Data-Centric Security
sections.content:
Data-centric security describes protections that remain with a Data packet wherever it is stored or retrieved. Integrity checks whether the packet changed; authenticity checks its name-to-content binding under a selected trust model.

Confidentiality is optional and includes protecting the content and hiding information in the name. The RFC notes that NDN and CCNx generally treat confidentiality as an application-layer concern rather than a network-layer service.
sections.plainLanguage: A Data packet can carry cryptographic protection that remains with it while it moves or is cached. That protection can verify integrity and authenticity, while confidentiality is generally handled by the application.
